scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire document (Pike et al., Prev Chronic Dis 2023) is a CDC-authored claims-based study estimating direct medical costs associated with post-COVID-19 conditions (PCC) among privately insured children and adults; Lyme disease is never mentioned anywhere in the text.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This CDC study used a large US commercial insurance claims database (IQVIA PharMetrics Plus) to compare medical spending, starting 31 days after diagnosis, between people diagnosed with COVID-19 (April-August 2020) and matched people without a COVID-19 diagnosis. It found that both children and adults with COVID-19 had meaningfully higher medical costs over the following 1, 3, and 6 months than their matched controls, with the largest relative cost gap among children and the largest dollar gap among adults aged 50-64 and among anyone previously hospitalized for COVID-19. The study only measures direct medical (claims) costs for privately insured people under 65 during the first pandemic year, before vaccines, Delta/Omicron, or a dedicated PCC diagnosis code existed, and explicitly does not estimate out-of-pocket cost differences or productivity/caregiving losses. The authors describe their approach as a likely lower-bound estimate of PCC-related health care utilization cost because no PCC-specific ICD-10 code was available during the study period.

contextual_issues: Out-of-pocket cost burden specific to PCC is mentioned as a gap but not separately estimated by this study; the reported direct medical costs already combine payer- and patient-paid amounts.
Productivity losses for patients or caregivers after a COVID-19 diagnosis are explicitly noted as not captured by this study.

A cited workers' compensation claims study (Bernacki et al., not this document's own data) is referenced as suggesting substantial costs attributable to a small subgroup of patients with prolonged disability after COVID-19, but this document does not quantify that itself.
As of July 2021, PCC could be considered a disability under the Americans with Disabilities Act - mentioned as policy context, not quantified as a cost.

An NIH initiative with $1.15 billion in congressional support (announced early 2021) to study PCC causes/treatment is mentioned as research-funding context, not used to compute any cost estimate in this study.
Caregiver time and repeated care-seeking patterns associated with PCC are not described or measured in this document beyond the aggregate cost figures.
evidence_gaps: Out-of-pocket cost differences specifically attributable to PCC (isolated from total payer+patient expenditure) are not estimated and would require claims data broken out by payment source.
Productivity loss and caregiver time/cost data are absent; would require linked employment, wage-replacement, or time-use data.
Costs beyond 6 months (longer-term/chronic PCC trajectories) are not modeled; would require longer follow-up in claims data.
Costs for Medicare, Medicaid, or uninsured populations, and for adults 65+, are not available since the data source is privately insured individuals under 65 only.

Cost profiles for Delta/Omicron-era infections and for vaccinated individuals are not available since the study period (April-August 2020 index dates) predates vaccination availability and later variants.
Socioeconomic, racial, and ethnic cost differences could not be assessed because the data source lacked these variables, despite documented early pandemic disparities in COVID-19 impact.

Because no PCC-specific ICD-10 code (U09.9) existed during the study period, cases were identified by proxy (COVID-19 diagnosis plus elevated post-acute costs) rather than directly coded PCC diagnoses; a replication using U09.9-coded cohorts would be needed to assess how this affects the estimates.
comparison_boundaries: Child and adult cost models use different age-group covariates and were estimated in separate 2-part models; their excess-cost dollar figures should not be pooled into one all-ages average.
The 1-, 3-, and 6-month cost windows are cumulative totals starting 31 days after the index date (not independent, sequential monthly costs) - they overlap and cannot be summed as additive periods.

Direct medical cost figures already represent total expenditures paid by both payer and patient combined; the document explicitly treats out-of-pocket burden as a separate, unestimated category - it must not be added again on top of these total-expenditure figures.

The $47 million (children) and $308 million (adults) aggregate figures apply only to this specific matched study cohort (209,048 matched groups, April-August 2020 index dates) and are not a national or annual population-wide estimate.

scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire document (Pike et al., Prev Chronic Dis 2023) is a CDC-authored claims-based study estimating direct medical costs associated with post-COVID-19 conditions (PCC) among privately insured children and adults; Lyme disease is never mentioned anywhere in the text.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This CDC study used a large US commercial insurance claims database (IQVIA PharMetrics Plus) to compare medical spending, starting 31 days after diagnosis, between people diagnosed with COVID-19 (April-August 2020) and matched people without a COVID-19 diagnosis. It found that both children and adults with COVID-19 had meaningfully higher medical costs over the following 1, 3, and 6 months than their matched controls, with the largest relative cost gap among children and the largest dollar gap among adults aged 50-64 and among anyone previously hospitalized for COVID-19. The study only measures direct medical (claims) costs for privately insured people under 65 during the first pandemic year, before vaccines, Delta/Omicron, or a dedicated PCC diagnosis code existed, and explicitly does not estimate out-of-pocket cost differences or productivity/caregiving losses. The authors describe their approach as a likely lower-bound estimate of PCC-related health care utilization cost because no PCC-specific ICD-10 code was available during the study period.

spec.title: Post-COVID-19 Excess Direct Medical Cost Explorer (Privately Insured, 2020 Cohort)
spec.boundary: This simulation reproduces the CDC/Pike et al. (2023) comparison of total direct medical claims costs (combined insurer- and patient-paid amounts) between privately insured people diagnosed with COVID-19 in April-August 2020 and matched people without a diagnosis, over the 6 months starting 31 days after diagnosis. It covers only people under 65 with commercial insurance, only the pre-vaccine, pre-Delta/Omicron period, and only direct medical claims costs. It does not estimate out-of-pocket spending separately, productivity or caregiving losses, costs beyond 6 months, costs for Medicare/Medicaid/uninsured populations, or costs for later pandemic periods.

takeaway.patient: A 2023 CDC study compared medical claims costs for privately insured children and adults diagnosed with COVID-19 in 2020 (before vaccines existed) to similar people without a COVID-19 diagnosis. Over the following six months, both diagnosed children and adults had higher total medical costs (combined insurer- and patient-paid amounts, not just what a person pays out of pocket) than their matched comparison groups, with children showing a larger percentage increase and adults a larger dollar increase. People who were hospitalized for COVID-19 had far higher follow-up costs than those who were not. These are claims-based patterns from one 2020 study population under 65 with private insurance, not a prediction of any individual's bill.
takeaway.care: This CDC claims-based analysis found that both pediatric and adult COVID-19 patients had significantly higher 6-month downstream medical costs than matched non-COVID controls, with hospitalized patients showing dramatically higher subsequent costs (about 3x for adults, about 9x for children) than non-hospitalized patients with a COVID-19 diagnosis. The sex-based cost difference among adults is nuanced: men's dollar cost gap was significantly higher at 1 and 3 months but not at 6 months, while the relative (percentage) cost increase remained significantly higher for men through 6 months. ## Source and scope
This simulator is based on Pike et al. (CDC, Preventing Chronic Disease, 2023), a claims-based study using IQVIA PharMetrics Plus commercial insurance data. Cases are privately insured children (0-17) and adults (18-64) with a COVID-19 diagnosis (ICD-10 code U07.1) with an index date between April and August 2020, matched 4:1 to people without a COVID-19 diagnosis. All dollar figures are 2020 total direct medical expenditures - combined amounts paid by insurer and patient together, measured from 31 days to 6 months after the index date. The study does not separate out-of-pocket spending from insurer-paid spending, so that split cannot be shown here, and patient payments are never added on top of these totals.

## Inputs and outputs
Input defaults are the study's own reported excess-cost and cost-multiplier figures (Table 2, p.9; Table 3, p.10; Table 4, p.11). Slider ranges beyond each default are assumed exploration bounds chosen for this simulator, not reported uncertainty intervals, and are noted per input. The male-minus-female output preserves a distinction the document itself makes: at 6 months, the absolute dollar gap between men ($1,764) and women ($1,530) was not statistically significant, while the relative (percentage) increase was significantly higher for men (about 1.59x vs. 1.41x) - these measure different things and neither supersedes the other. The hospitalization multipliers show how much higher 6-month costs were for patients hospitalized during their COVID-19 episode versus those who were not.

## Limitations
No post-COVID-19 condition (PCC)-specific diagnosis code existed during the study period (the general code U09.9 took effect in October 2021); the authors identified likely PCC cases indirectly by comparing costs of diagnosed patients to matched controls and describe their result as a likely lower bound on PCC-related cost, since some true cases could go uncaptured and some matched controls could include undiagnosed COVID-19. This reflects a limitation of the evidence system itself - without a dedicated diagnosis code, claims-based PCC cost tracking generally understates true utilization - separate from the accuracy of any single estimate here.

The study's cohort-level aggregate figures (reported by the authors as up to about $47 million for children and $308 million for adults, within this one 2020 matched cohort only) were presented as single pooled totals without breakdown by sex, age, or race/ethnicity, even though the per-person figures used elsewhere in this simulator were disaggregated by sex and age. Federal survey sources such as NHIS and BRFSS generally support disaggregated analyses even though this study did not perform one for its aggregate totals.

Findings apply only to privately insured people under 65 during the unvaccinated, pre-Delta/Omicron period of 2020 and do not generalize to Medicare, Medicaid, or uninsured populations, later pandemic periods, or vaccinated individuals. Productivity loss and caregiving costs are not captured anywhere in this data.
